notes.meaning: Zophar the Naamathite steps forward to speak a second time. Provoked by Job's warnings of judgment, he interrupts and responds with renewed heat and urgency.
Zophar admits that an inner agitation drives him to answer immediately. His racing thoughts and troubled feelings will not let him stay silent.
Zophar feels stung and insulted by Job's sharp rebukes of the three friends. He claims his own understanding now compels him to defend himself and speak the truth.
Zophar appeals to what humans have known from the very beginning of history. He asks Job if he has forgotten this age-old rule that has stood since people were placed on earth.
Zophar insists that the celebration of the wicked never lasts very long. Any joy a hypocrite or godless person experiences will quickly vanish.
A wicked person may rise to great power and lift his head high into the clouds with pride. Yet no amount of worldly honor can protect him from coming down.
In the end, the proud sinner will perish forever, treated with utter disgust like household waste. Those who once looked up to him will look around and ask where he went.
The sinner will disappear completely, like a dream that vanishes the moment someone wakes up. He is chased away like a fleeting shadow in the night and cannot be found again.
The eyes that once watched him go about his daily life will never see him again. Even the place where he lived will forget him, showing how completely his presence is wiped out.
The oppressor's children will be brought so low that they must beg for kindness from the very poor he mistreated. What the father stole by force will have to be restored to its rightful owners.
Even if a wicked man is still in the prime of his youthful strength, death will bring him down. His vigorous body will lie in the dust, cut down early by the results of his wrongdoing.
Zophar compares sin to a sweet treat that delights an evil person's taste. The sinner keeps it under his tongue, rolling it around so the pleasure will last longer.
The wicked man loves his evil ways too much to give them up or spit them out. He clings to his sin tightly and cherishes it inside his mouth.
Although evil tastes pleasant going down, it soon turns sour in the stomach. The sin becomes deadly poison inside him, like the venom of an angry cobra.
The wicked man swallows down wealth that belongs to others, but he cannot keep it. God Himself will make him vomit it back up, forcing him to surrender what he stole.
The evil gains that seemed so sweet will prove to be deadly snake venom. What the sinner took in will destroy him from within, as if bitten by a viper.

The wicked person will never get to enjoy the rich, overflowing blessings of life. Zophar pictures these lost blessings as flowing streams of milk and sweet honey, which God withholds from the wicked.
The oppressor must give back the fruit of all his hard labor without getting to enjoy it. He will not be allowed to celebrate or keep the profits he made from his dealings.
This judgment comes upon him because he mistreated the helpless and left the poor with nothing. He broke down homes and took houses he never built, acting only for himself.
Because his greed was never satisfied, he never felt true peace or contentment within himself. In the end, his restless craving cannot save a single thing he treasured.
He devoured everything so greedily that nothing was left over for anyone else. Because of this cruel selfishness, his prosperity will vanish and leave nothing behind.
Even when he has plenty of everything, deep anxiety and trouble will hem him in. The full weight of misery, and the retaliation of those he wronged, will crash down upon him.
When the sinner sits down to satisfy his desires, God sends burning anger against him. God rains judgment down upon him like a terrible storm while he is still feasting.
If the wicked man manages to run away from an iron weapon, an arrow shot from a bronze bow strikes him down. He cannot escape God's judgment, because dodging one threat only walks him into another.
The arrow is pulled out of his back, its shining point stained with bodily fluid from a fatal wound. Overwhelming dread falls upon him as he faces certain death.
Total darkness and ruin are kept in store for all his hidden treasures. A fire kindled by no human hand—God's own wrath—will burn him up and destroy whatever remains in his tent.
The heavens will expose his hidden sins, and the earth itself will rise up in opposition to him. All of creation joins together to witness against the wicked man and ensure his downfall.
All the wealth and goods stored in the sinner's house will be swept away like floodwaters. When the day of God's anger arrives, everything he owned will be carried off and lost.
Zophar concludes that this terrible fate is the exact portion God assigns to every wicked person. God has decreed this ruin as their settled heritage.
